subject: Science
central_question: How do the physical properties, chemical reactivity, bonding, occurrence, extraction and corrosion of metals and non-metals explain their behaviour and uses?
in_scope_units: Physical properties of metals: lustre, hardness, malleability, ductility, heat and electrical conductivity, and sonority
Physical properties of non-metals and important exceptions to general metal/non-metal trends
Chemical properties of metals with oxygen, water, dilute acids and salt solutions
The reactivity series and prediction of displacement reactions
Electron transfer between metals and non-metals and the formation of ionic compounds
Physical properties, solubility and electrical conductivity of ionic compounds
Occurrence of metals as minerals and ores, enrichment of ores and extraction according to reactivity
Roasting, calcination, reduction, thermit reaction, electrolytic reduction and electrolytic refining
Corrosion of silver, copper and iron, conditions required for rusting, and methods of prevention
Alloys, amalgams and the improvement of metal properties
banned_topics: Detailed periodic-table classification and periodic trends
Carbon compound nomenclature and homologous series
Detailed electrochemical-cell theory beyond the electrolytic processes described in this chapter

known_pitfalls.claim: Every metal is hard, solid and has a high melting point.
known_pitfalls.correction: These are general trends with exceptions: mercury is liquid at room temperature, gallium and caesium have low melting points, and alkali metals such as sodium are soft enough to cut with a knife.

known_pitfalls.claim: All metal oxides are only basic.
known_pitfalls.correction: Most metal oxides are basic, but aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are amphoteric because they react with both acids and bases to form salt and water.

known_pitfalls.claim: Any metal can displace any other metal from its salt solution.
known_pitfalls.correction: A displacement occurs only when the free metal is more reactive than the metal present in the salt solution.

known_pitfalls.claim: Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the solid state because they contain ions.
known_pitfalls.correction: Their ions are fixed in a rigid lattice in the solid state; ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved in water because the ions can then move.

known_pitfalls.claim: Rusting needs only water or only oxygen.
known_pitfalls.correction: Activity 3.14 shows that iron rusts when both air and water are present.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Activities 3.1-3.7 to classify samples by lustre, malleability, ductility, conductivity and sonority while noting exceptions.
Use NCERT Activities 3.9-3.12 to infer relative reactivity from reactions with oxygen, water, acids and salt solutions.
Use NCERT Figures 3.5-3.6 and Activity 3.13 to explain electron transfer and the properties of ionic compounds.
Use NCERT Figure 3.10 and the extraction examples for mercury, copper and zinc to select a metallurgy method from the reactivity series.
Use NCERT Activity 3.14 and Exercise Questions 2, 10 and 12 to reason about corrosion and its prevention.
